figures.caption: Figure 1: The evidential chain studied in this paper. Each stage has a different observable and a different failure mode. The arrows denote evaluation order, not logical implication.
Table 1: Recovery and forecasting on the common cohort. “Recoverable error” restricts structural error to trajectories favorable under the task-specific recoverability measure. Lower is better.

Figure 2: Stage-I calibration. P1 empirical reference error tracks analytic Bayes risk; P2 error decreases with nuisance-profile separation; P3 structural error is ordered by numerical Bayes risk. P2 is an ordering diagnostic rather than a Bayes identity.
Table 5: Exact-tier theory-calibration checks. Error is the observed fraction of wrong delay or kernel selections.
Table 10: Exact-tier functional consistency. Gaps are mean absolute distances between the reported delay (kernel peak for P3) and the functional response peak.
Table 11: P1 stress-tier functional consistency. The unused rate conditions on a correct structural report. Each model–tier cell uses 200 trajectories.

Table 12: Functional diagnostics on the strict Link-II cohort. Additive interventions use the same locked rows at all amplitudes; conditional replacement samples from the exact Gaussian input conditional.
Table 14: P1 loss-weight robustness. Increasing forecast weight improves MSE but reduces report accuracy and eligible-cohort size; gap/alignment measures nevertheless remain strongly separated.

Figure 3: Mechanism-specific robustness profiles; lower structural error is better. Top: 120 trajectories per severity show distinct degradation under P1 outliers, a P2 unmodeled dynamic term, and P3 sensor smoothing. Bottom: cascades, parallel paths, and sensor dynamics compare correlation rules with a simulator-matched candidate MLE. Empirical zeros indicate no errors in the finite sample, not zero population risk; matched MLE is a generator-aware sanity reference rather than a general-purpose model.
Table 19: Structural recovery across training budgets with architecture, optimization protocol, test cohort, and seeds fixed. Values are separate-head means; lower error is better.
Table 22: Complete unified common-cohort results; unsupported structural outputs are dashes. Neural entries average three seeds.
Table 26: Fresh-B ten-seed replication with a prospective-seven sensitivity analysis. Effects are coupled minus uncoupled.
Table 27: Individual-seed Fresh-B primary effects. Coupled minus uncoupled; negative gap and positive alignment are favorable. Both endpoints favor routing in all ten seeds for both backbones.

Table 28: Five-arm Fresh-B mechanism decomposition. Arm A is uncoupled; B applies the uncoupled model’s own gate only at evaluation time; C is coupled-trained. Shuffle and permute keep the original declared report fixed while destroying gate-to-coordinate correspondence.

Table 29: Full paired mechanism decomposition. B−A is the post-hoc gate effect, C−A the total trained coupled-minus-uncoupled effect, and C−B the beyond-post-hoc contrast. The last two columns are gatedestruction controls relative to C.

Table 32: P1 routing mechanism test on the common cohort. Structural error and forecast MSE are lower-isbetter; fixed report–use gap is in lags, with 0 meaning exact peak alignment under the fixed-report intervention.

Table 35: Release and cohort map. Comparisons are paired only within a row; independent releases are not pooled for ranking. “Replay” means evaluation of frozen predictions or deterministic rules without retraining.

Table 36: Run accounting by scientific study. Training, calibration-probe fits, checkpoint/rule evaluations, and bootstrap analyses are distinct operations; scientific aggregates use the completed runs specified by each study contract.
